The Ashʿarite idea of repeated creation rests on the principle that an accident does not last for two moments, while creation itself is an accident. Creation must therefore be continually repeated. This idea contains an unintended materialist implication because it leads to the eternity of the world. If creation is continually repeated, the world exists for as long as God exists. If the world came to an end, that would mean God had ceased to be a creator. The Ashʿarites, of course, cannot accept that conclusion. They therefore face a contradiction with only two possible solutions: either accept the eternity of the world, in keeping with belief in God’s eternity, or reject the idea of continuous repeated creation.↩︎

Detailed explanations of the Ashʿarite position on this question can be found in the works of major Ashʿarite thinkers, especially Abū Bakr al-Ṭayyib al-Bāqillānī, or Ibn al-Bāqillānī (d. 403 AH/1012 CE), in al-Tamhīd fī al-Radd ʿalā al-Muʿaṭṭila wa-l-Rāfiḍa, and Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, especially in The Incoherence of the Philosophers.↩︎

By “metaphysical” here, we mean the opposite of “dialectical.” Denying causality in the relationships between natural and social phenomena amounts to treating the universe as static. It also means denying the law of development, which is connected to a chain of causes, conditions, and chance events produced by the dialectical motion of matter in the universe. The static character comes from the idea that, at every moment and in every part of their existence, things require outside intervention through the process of continual renewed creation. Existence in itself is therefore motionless and cannot move for even a moment without an external mover. This is so even though, as noted earlier, the idea of continuously renewed creation can also lead in another direction to a materialist position.↩︎
ʿAlī Sāmī al-Nashshār, Methods of Research among Muslim Thinkers, Dār al-Maʿārif, Cairo, 1965, p. 168.↩︎

The Arabic word manṭiq (“logic”) is a verbal noun from naṭaqa, meaning to speak aloud using sounds and letters that convey meaning. Arab scholars of rhetoric also used manṭiq to mean speech or expression. Ibn al-Sikkīt, for example, called his book Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq, meaning the correction or refinement of expression and eloquent speech. In most later usage, however, the word came to mean the “science of logic” (Logic).↩︎

In the introduction to the second edition of Philosophical Notebooks, Lenin discusses the relationship between thought and language while commenting on Hegel’s remarks in his Logic about “detached forms of thought.” Hegel notes that German contains words that sometimes have opposing meanings. Lenin comments: not merely “different” meanings, but opposing ones. Hegel continues: “That is a delight for thought.” Lenin then writes in the margin: “History of thought = history of language.” See the Arabic edition of Philosophical Notebooks.↩︎

As noted earlier, Aristotle was unable to solve the problem of how thought moves from individual cases to the universal that includes them. In other words, he could not explain the real relationship between the universal and the individual, or establish how the connections between concepts correspond to the connections found in the sensory world. In fact, this problem remained unresolved until Marxist philosophy found its answer by discovering the active social essence of human beings. Through practical activity, within people’s social life, the relationship between the universal and the individual becomes clear. A human being is a social being, and each individual human is both an individual and a member of the universal or general category. The universal therefore exists in the individual: the existence of the individual contains the existence of the universal. The individual comes first, and the universal arises on the basis of individual existence. Darwin’s theory can provide a scientific and practical example of how a “universal” arises in a new biological species of animal or plant. According to Darwin’s theory, accidental changes occur in a group of individual organisms. From these changes a new species emerges, and with that species comes the general concept that refers to it.↩︎
